newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries open down, new Yellen article cited.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries open down, new Yellen article cited.

text.p: U.S. Treasury prices opened lower on Wednesday with a fresh reminder of Federal Reserve policy makers' fears that rising labor costs could set off a gradual rise in inflation.

"There was a Washington Post John Berry story that seems to have said all the obvious things -- that the Fed is worried about labor costs slowly, gradually translating into higher inflation and that it is contemplating a 25 basis point tightening in September," said Josh Stiles, senior bond strategist at I.D.E.A.
Fed Governor Janet Yellen told the Post, "'I find myself nervous about the diminishing slack in the labor market. I think we are in an inflationary danger zone."
Yellen's reference to an inflationary danger zone echoed her remarks published by Reuters on Tuesday. Those comments were widely cited as the cause of the market's decline that day.

The Washington Post column said labor costs were crucial to the inflation puzzle. It said "some Fed policymakers are puzzled" as to why the nation's sustained low unemployment rate -- it was down to 5.1 percent (in August) -- hasn't already triggered a slow but steady rise in inflation.

"That's one reason why they are pondering whether they should try to cool the economy down a bit by raising short-term interest rates at a a policymaking session Sept. 24," the Washington Post article said.
Other contributors to the market's weak open included some weakness overseas as people shortened up on the curve.
"There was some swap-related activity," Stiles said. "Somebody got rid of some five-years."
The market's only fresh economic report on Wednesday is the Federal Reserve Beige Book, due at 1200 EDT/1600 GMT.
The Beige Book, sometimes called the Tan Book, is an anecdotal description of business conditions around the nation culled by the 12 regional banks of the Federal Reserve.
"The Beige Book will certainly be the market focus today, (aside from comments from Federal Reserve officials)," said James Blumenthal, economist at MCM Moneywatch.

"The market is going to be alert to any description of wage pressures (in the Beige Book)," said Stiles. "We don't expect it to report a sudden escalation in wage gains and we think the overall picture (the Beige Book paints) will be moderately upbeat for the economy."

"The market will pay particular attention to what the Beige Book says about inflation and the labor markets and to the extent of which it sees signs of wage pressures -- whether they are scattered or pervasive -- and to whether it talks about the economy softening from the second quarter," said Blumenthal.
But the market is also focused on economic data not due until Thursday and Friday, analysts said.
The government will report on August wholesale price trends on Thursday and consumer prices and retail sales on Friday.
Economists Reuters polled expect both the core and total Producer Price Index (PPI) to be up 0.1 percent on Thursday.
Economists expect both the core and overall August Consumer Price Index (CPI) on Friday to be up 0.2 percent.
"If you get a 0.3 percent rise or higher in the core CPI, that's where the market starts to have a stomach ache," said Stiles.
In early trade, the 6-3/4 percent 30-year bond was down 8/32 to 95-9/32, yielding 7.13 percent.
At the short end of the maturity range, the three- and six-month Treasury bill rates were each up one basis point to 5.16 percent and 5.34 percent, respectively.

The two-year note was down 1/32 to 99-19/32, yielding 6.35 percent. The five-year note was down 3/32 to 99-3/32, yielding 6.72 percent, and the 10-year note was down 5/32 to 100-11/32, yielding 6.95 percent.
